title: How Long Can Food Stay Out of the Refrigerator?

seo.title: How Long Food Can Stay Out of the Refrigerator
seo.meta_description: Perishable food should not stay unrefrigerated for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90 °F / 32 °C. Learn which foods this applies to and when food should be discarded.
seo.search_intent: Know how long perishable food can safely remain at room temperature and when it is no longer safe to refrigerate it again.

excerpt: Perishable food should not remain out of refrigeration for more than two hours. If the surrounding temperature is above 90 °F / 32 °C, the limit drops to one hour. This applies to meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, dairy, leftovers and other foods that require refrigeration. Once that time has been exceeded, putting the food back in the refrigerator does not restore the lost safety margin.
content_html:
A pizza on the table, a pot of rice after dinner or a tray of chicken at a party all raise the same question: how long can food safely stay out of the refrigerator?

For perishable food, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) uses a rule that is easy to remember: no more than two hours at room temperature, or one hour when the temperature is above 90 °F / 32 °C.

The reason is not that food suddenly changes appearance at the two-hour mark. It is that between 40 and 140 °F—about 4.4 to 60 °C—many microorganisms can multiply rapidly.

The two-hour rule applies to foods that need refrigeration

Not every pantry food needs to race back into the refrigerator. Bread, crackers, whole uncut fruit and other shelf-stable foods may have different storage requirements.

The rule is especially important for meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, milk and other dairy products, cooked food, leftovers and anything whose label says to keep refrigerated.

The time is cumulative

If a chicken salad sits out for 45 minutes, goes back into the refrigerator and then later spends another hour on the table, those warm periods are not completely independent. The food has repeatedly spent time in a temperature range that supports bacterial growth.

For long meals or buffets, a safer strategy is to put out small amounts and replenish from refrigerated storage instead of leaving the entire batch on the table for hours.

In hot weather, one hour goes quickly

USDA reduces the limit to one hour when the ambient temperature exceeds 90 °F / 32 °C. That matters at picnics, barbecues, in cars, on sunny patios and in very hot kitchens.

A closed car can become much hotter than the outdoor air. Do not treat the trunk or back seat as temporary refrigerated storage.

What if food has been out three hours but still feels cool?

Touch cannot accurately measure food temperature or reconstruct how long the food spent in the danger zone. A container may feel cool outside while warmer areas existed inside.

Once a perishable food has clearly exceeded the recommended time, cooling it again does not reset the clock.

Smell is not a safety test either

Many disease-causing microorganisms do not produce noticeable odors, flavors or visible changes. Food can smell perfectly normal after spending too long at room temperature.

Tasting a bite to test it adds exposure rather than providing reliable information.

Hot food is covered by the rule too

A casserole is not protected forever just because it came out of a hot oven. If it is not being held at a safe hot temperature, it begins cooling into the range where microbial growth can speed up.

If it will not be served promptly, either keep it hot under controlled conditions or cool and refrigerate it quickly.

Do not wait for a large pot to become completely cold

Leaving a big batch on the counter for several hours because you do not want to “put hot food in the fridge” can prolong exactly the temperature exposure you are trying to avoid.

Divide soups, stews, rice and other large preparations into shallow containers so they lose heat more quickly during cooling and refrigeration.

What about pizza?

Pizza with cheese, meat or other perishable toppings follows the same time-and-temperature principle as other cooked foods. The fact that people commonly leave the box out during a party does not change the food-safety rule.

If you want to keep the remaining slices, refrigerate them within the safe window rather than leaving them on the counter overnight.

What about eggs, milk and yogurt?

In markets where these products are sold refrigerated, they should remain cold. USDA includes eggs and dairy among perishable foods that should not sit at room temperature for hours.

Practices can differ between countries for certain eggs or processed products, so follow the label and the storage chain used in your market as well.

For outdoor meals, use active cooling

A cooler works best when it is well packed with ice or frozen cold packs and opened infrequently. Keeping drinks separate from food can help reduce how often the food cooler is opened.

In hot weather, shade is not a substitute for refrigeration. Shade reduces direct heating but does not keep food at 40 °F / 4.4 °C by itself.

If food was unrefrigerated because the power went out

A power outage is different from leaving a plate on the table because a closed refrigerator can stay cold for a period of time. Keep the door closed and use a thermometer when possible to understand what temperature the food actually reached.

The decision afterward depends on real time and temperature, not just how long the outage lasted.

What if you do not know how long the food has been out?

If you arrive at a gathering and cannot tell whether a meat dish, salad or cooked food has been out for 20 minutes or four hours, you do not have a reliable time history.

For higher-risk foods, especially when serving young children, pregnant people, older adults or anyone with a weakened immune system, a conservative decision is appropriate.

The rule that solves most situations

Perishable food: no more than two hours out of refrigeration, or one hour when the temperature is above 90 °F / 32 °C. After that, do not try to “save” it simply by chilling it again.

Refrigeration preserves food that is still within a safe handling history; it cannot undo hours already spent at an unsafe temperature.

faq.question: How long can food stay at room temperature?
faq.answer: Perishable food should not remain out for more than two hours, or one hour when the temperature is above 90 °F / 32 °C.

faq.question: Can I refrigerate food again after it has been out for three hours?
faq.answer: For perishable food, clearly exceeding the two-hour rule means chilling it again does not restore the lost safety margin.

faq.question: Can pizza stay out overnight?
faq.answer: It is not recommended. Pizza with perishable toppings should be refrigerated within the safe time window.

faq.question: Can smell tell me whether food left out is safe?
faq.answer: No. Illness-causing microorganisms can grow without changing smell, taste or appearance.
